chapter: Building McShann's big band and blues records
title: Charlie Parker before and after George E. Lee: 'Lady Be Good'
summary: Ramey knew Bird from 1934 as a poor player; he returned in 1937 playing Lester Young's solo note for note.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Well, listen, before Bird went down to the Ozarks with George E. Lee, now, according to Jay, when he comes back, he's really changed a lot.

Yeah, definitely. Well, now, you see, actually, I have to say that I don't think Jay knew him before that because Jay hadn't come to Kansas City. Jay was there when he came back, and Parker met him maybe because he left -- that was in '36 and Jay came in '36. But, say, like, the times when we knew him -- I knew him from early '34, when he was a nothing saxophone player, and we used to go to jam sessions. I used to get him out of there and make him go home and so forth.
Maybe -- of course, that's what Jay meant. He may have meant that he --
He probably had heard the rumor about how bad --

Yeah, he was a terrible saxophone player. But back in those days, I could always get him to jam with me. And even when we got with Mashann, when I saw he was getting ready to go get himself some drugs or something, I'd tell him, Man, can't you give me 15 minutes, just kind of get
our fingers together?" He'd get down there and I started playing and forget all about those things.

But, now, that thing (unintelligible) is definitely true. When he came back from George F. Lee, and by that time that Jones Smith record had come out, Basie, so that might have been in early '37 because Basie left in '36.

Yeah. Well, that Jones-Smith record come out and Prez had made that 'Lady Be Good.' And Bird came back and he startled everybody. He hit 'Lady Be Good,' and all the other saxophone players played, and the cats said, yeah, here come this guy, he's a drag. He gets up and plays Lester Young's solo note for note.
Played it note for note, sounded just '... dig that man.' like Prez. And from then on, Bird was gone.
He played it on alto, then.
Yeah, note for note. Couldn't believe that. Six months before that, he was, like, a crying saxophone player. Although he had improved from when I heard him in '34.
